list-item.p: The tandem CD20/CD19 CAR T-cell product zamto-cel is well tolerated in a phase 1 trial of R/R B-NHL.
Long-term responses up to 5 years were accompanied by expression of CD27 and CD127 along with increased expansion of CAR+ TCM cells.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Emerging long-term data indicate relapse rates of >50% after CD19-redirected chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in relapsed or refractory (R/R) B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-NHL). To reduce selective pressure on the CD19 antigen, we conducted a first-in-human phase 1 clinical trial of zamtocabtagene autoleucel (zamto-cel), a noncryopreserved tandem CD20-CD19–directed CAR T-cell therapy. Two predefined dose levels (dose level 1 [DL1], 1 × 106 and DL2, 2.5 × 106 CAR+ T cells per kg bodyweight) were applied. The primary end point (EP) was the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary EPs included adverse events, best overall response (BOR), and biomarker assessments. A total of 12 patients, 6 patients per DL, were treated. No dose-limiting toxicity and no cytokine release syndrome or immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome of grade ≥3 were observed. Thus, MTD was not reached. The BOR by investigator assessment was 75%, with 5 of 12 patients (42%) achieving complete remission (CR) until month 12 with no relapse in clinical evaluation up to 5 years after infusion. CR was associated with a higher mean maximum observed concentration of zamto-cel and detection of zamto-cel beyond month 6. Additional product characterization revealed increased expression of CD27 and CD127 along with increased expansion of CAR+ central memory T cells in patients with CR, facilitating persistence and improved outcomes in R/R B-NHL treated with zamto-cel. Based on the promising risk-to-benefit ratio, evaluation of zamto-cel at DL2 is ongoing in pivotal phase 2 clinical trials for patients with R/R aggressive B-NHL. This trial was registered at www.ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT03870945.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy directed against CD19 has heralded a new era in the treatment of relapsed/refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (R/R B-NHL).1,2 Long-term follow-up of the pivotal ZUMA-1 trial has shown that only 31% of patients remain in remission after 5 years.3 Resistance to anti-CD19 CAR T cells has been attributed to several factors: limited CAR T-cell activity due to T-cell exhaustion,4 accompanied by poor persistence,5 as well as tumor-driven mechanisms such as an immunosuppressive microenvironment6, 7, 8, 9 and downregulation or even loss of the target antigen.10,11 Targeting a single antigen leads to selective pressure and thus facilitates antigen loss.12 Therefore, generating multispecific CAR T cells provides an exciting avenue to bolster efficacy. Successfully engineering multispecific CARs with equivalent potency across targets is challenging.13,14 The tandem CAR targeting CD20 and CD19 (pLTG1497) has previously shown robust antilymphoma activity15 and mitigated downregulation of B-cell antigens.16 Clinical evidence suggests that dual targeting of CD20 and CD19 is safe because off-tumor toxicity for both antigens is limited to B cells,17,18 with manageable long-term effects of prolonged B-cell aplasia.19

It is well established that a less-differentiated cell state yields enhanced engraftment of adoptive T-cell therapies.20,21 In CAR T-cell products, the proportion of memory T cells influences their clinical efficacy.22, 23, 24 CD27 is known as a costimulator of T-cell expansion; however, it does not induce effector cell differentiation. Thus, CD27 takes a central role in T-cell memory formation and persistence.25,26 Tumor-specific T-cell persistence can be further enhanced by the cytokine interleukin-7 (IL-7),27 and genetically engineered T-cell therapies either secreting IL-7 or overexpressing the IL-7 receptor (IL-7R [CD127]) have been shown to result in improved antitumor reactivity.28,29

We conducted a phase 1 clinical study of autologous pLTG1497-transduced CAR T cells (zamtocabtagene autoleucel [zamto-cel]) manufactured in a 12-day process without cryopreservation on the CliniMACS Prodigy. This manufacturing approach was 2 days shorter than previous processes and avoided the need for cryopreservation.15 Here, we report safety, preliminary efficacy evaluated with a follow-up of 5 years, and in-depth product characterization along with in vivo profiling of zamto-cel. Importantly, complete remission (CR) in patients was not associated with dose level (DL) but with in vivo expansion and persistence of zamto-cel. Subsequent profiling of preinfusion drug product (DP) from patients with CR not only revealed higher levels of central memory (CD62L+/CD45RO+) CAR T cells but also increased levels of CD27 and CD127/IL-7R, facilitating memory formation, and enhanced zamto-cel persistence.

sec.title: Study design and patient population
sec.p: We conducted a prospective, multicenter, open-label phase 1 first-in-human clinical trial to evaluate feasibility, dosage, efficacy, safety, and toxicity of treatment with ex vivo expanded autologous T cells genetically modified to express a CD20 and CD19 tandem CAR (zamto-cel)16 in patients with R/R B-NHL (supplemental Figure 1). Two predefined DLs were investigated in 2 cohorts using a 6+3 trial design. Cohort 1 (DL1) was treated with 1 × 106 CAR+ T cells per kg bodyweight, and cohort 2 (DL2) with 2.5 × 106 CAR+ T cells per kg bodyweight.

Key eligibility criteria included histologically confirmed B-NHL, measurable disease per positron emission tomography–computed tomography as per the Lugano classification30 and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 0 to 2. Specifically, in DL1, patients with R/R CD20+ and CD19+ B-NHL and no available approved standard therapy were included, whereas DL2 was restricted to patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), R/R after only 1 treatment line, who were not eligible for high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation. A positivity for CD19 and CD20 (by flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry) was no longer required. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in supplemental Information 1.

Informed consent was obtained from each patient before any study-related procedure. The study was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, International Council for Harmonization good clinical practice guidelines, and applicable regulatory requirements, and was approved by the responsible independent ethics committees. Adverse events (AE), including neurotoxicity reporting, was classified according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.31 Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) was graded using criteria from Lee et al32 and treated according to institutional guidelines.

sec.title: End points and statistical analysis
sec.p: The primary end points considered were the determination of the maximum tolerated dose as well as safety and toxicity assessment of zamto-cel per AE, reported according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.31 Maximum tolerated dose was defined as the DL at which <33% of patients experienced dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) until day 28 after infusion. Further information on end points and statistical analyses is included in supplemental Information 2.

sec.title: Manufacturing of zamto-cel and lymphodepletion
sec.p: Zamto-cel, a centrally manufactured product, was successfully produced for all 12 patients. The planned dose of the noncryopreserved product was produced on the fully automated CliniMACS Prodigy system with a production time of 12 days and administered to all patients IV. Median time from leukapheresis to reinfusion was 14 days (range, 13-14).

Lymphodepleting chemotherapy was administered IV from day −5 to day −3 before zamto-cel infusion and consisted of cyclophosphamide 300 mg/m2 body surface area (BSA) and fludarabine 30 mg/m2 BSA from day −5 to day −3 at DL1. To align the lymphodepletion regimen with the US protocol (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04792489), the cyclophosphamide dose was adjusted to 500 mg/m2 BSA per day for DL2. Further information on manufacturing, lymphodepletion chemotherapy, and laboratory measurements can be found in supplemental Information 2.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Between February and December 2019, 12 patients (6 at DL1 and 6 at DL2) were enrolled at 3 trial sites in Germany, and all underwent leukapheresis. Median age was 72 years (range, 20-78), 10 patients were aged >65 years, and 8 were aged >70 years. Histologies included DLBCL (n = 8), transformed follicular lymphoma (n = 2), primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (n = 1), and mantle cell lymphoma (n = 1). All participants (12/12 [100.0%]) presented with CD20+ histology, and 10/10 (100.0%) with CD19+ histology at screening (2 samples in DL2 were not analyzed for CD19). Nine (75.0%) patients had advanced Ann Arbor stage III/IV disease, 6 (50.0%) patients had refractory disease at study entry, and International Prognostic Index was ≥3 in 7 (58.3%) patients (Table 1; supplemental Table 1).

sec.p: The median follow-up time among patients was 24.6 months (range, 4.6-60.3). Six patients (3 in each DL) finished the active part of the study by completing the 1-year follow-up and continued to be followed up in the trial (3 of these 6 patients participated in the year 3 visit). Six patients, with documented R/R disease finished the trial prematurely due to withdrawal of consent (n = 4) or were lost to follow-up (n = 1), or died (n = 1; supplemental Figure 2).

sec.title: Zamto-cel manufacturing
sec.p: All leukapheresis products (LPs) showed similar CD3+ cell percentages of 39.9% ± 10.9% and all DPs had a high CD3+ cell purity (99.3% ± 0.7%) and viability (94.0% ± 3.1%; supplemental Figure 3A-B). Patients who achieved a CR had higher amounts of B cells in the LP than patients without CR (6.0 ± 3.9 vs 0.7 ± 1.3; supplemental Figure 3C). Mean transduction frequency was 18.0% (21.0% ± 4.8% in CR vs 15.9% ± 6.7% in non-CR; P = .19; supplemental Figure 3D). Although we observed a CD4:CD8 ratio of 1.5 ± 0.9 in the LP, we found a mean CD4:CD8 ratio of 4.5 in CAR+ cells (6.0 ± 4.5 in CR vs 3.5 ± 2.1 in non-CR; P = .19; supplemental Figure 3E). After CD4 and CD8 selection and addition of cytokines, DPs showed a consistent T-cell expansion of 10.5-fold ± 3.5-fold in CD3+ cells, 9.5-fold ± 3.2-fold in CAR+CD4+ cells, and 12.0-fold ± 4.5-fold in CAR+CD8+ cells, with no difference between patients with and without CR (supplemental Figure 3F-G).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: No DLT was observed at any DL. The incidence of AE was assessed as a secondary end point. All 12 patients (100.0%) experienced at least 1 grade ≥3 AE. The most common treatment-emergent AEs of any grade were CRS (58.3%), constipation (41.7%), and neutrophil count decrease (33.3%; Figure 1A). Overall, CRS occurred in 3 of 6 patients at DL1 (50.0%) and 4 of 6 patients at DL2 (67.0%). Two events of CRS were classified as grade 2, both at DL2, and all others as grade 1. One patient at DL2 received a total of 2 doses of tocilizumab for grade 2 CRS. The median time to onset of CRS after infusion with zamto-cel was 6 days (range, 0-9). All 7 patients (100.0%) had a complete resolution of CRS within a median duration of 3 days (range, 2-4).

sec.p: Two events of immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) of any grade were reported in 1 patient (8.3%). Both events were of grade 1 and occurred on day 1 to day 3 and on day 8 to day 9. Only the first episode required steroids (10 mg dexamethasone) due to concomitant CRS grade 1 at DL2, and symptoms fully resolved after treatment with dexamethasone. No patient required vasopressors. Neither CRS nor ICANS were associated with intensive care unit admission. One patient required intensive care unit admission on day +75 after intestinal perforation without evidence of recurrent disease. The event was considered related to the study drug, most probably due to the intestinal lymphoma responding to zamto-cel.

At screening, 10 of 12 patients showed B-cell aplasia (1 missing value), defined as <0.1 CD19+CD20+ cells per μL in the peripheral blood as determined by flow cytometry. By day 14, 10 patients showed B-cell aplasia (2 missing values). Three of 6 patients with analysis at month 6 showed normalized B-cell counts. At 1 year after investigational medicinal product (IMP) infusion, 3 of 5 patients with ongoing CR had normal B-cell counts. Analysis of immunoglobulin G levels were available in all patients. Hypogammaglobulinemia of <4 g/L was present in 4 patients at least once after infusion (supplemental Figure 4). One participant received IV immunoglobulin preparations. One participant experienced grade 4 neutropenia with a duration of 30 days starting at day +9 after zamto-cel administration. Prolonged grade 3 neutropenia (defined as present at day 28 after zamto-cel administration) was documented for 1 patient with a duration of 14 days. For both patients, no infections were reported during this period. No further episodes of any hematological toxicities were reported 90 days after treatment with zamto-cel (posttreatment AEs).

Five (41.7%) patients experienced 11 treatment-emergent infections of any grade with a median duration of 13 days (range, 4-107). Two patients experienced 5 infectious events of grade ≥3. Only one patient suffered from infectious complications considered to be related to the IMP (5 events). This patient was treated at DL1 and experienced a urinary tract infection (grade 3, not considered related to IMP, day 0), and later during the clinical course an abdominal infection (grade 3, day 57), followed by septic shock (grade 4, day 75) and pneumonia (grade 3, day 75), all of which were considered to be related to the IMP. Another patient at DL1 had a grade 3 catheter-related infection on day 10 not related to the IMP. There were no infectious events of grade ≥3 reported at DL2 (Figure 1A). Seven patients experienced an infection during B-cell aplasia. However, in all cases, B-cell aplasia was already present before or at the time of, zamto-cel treatment.

One patient at DL1 developed a grade 3 sarcoma 399 days after zamto-cel infusion, which was considered a posttreatment AE not related to the IMP. Two cases of death, which were considered unrelated to the IMP, occurred on study and were caused by disease progression (n = 1) 7.8 months after treatment with zamto-cel and cardiac failure (n = 1) 14.6 months after treatment with zamto-cel. The second patient had initially achieved a partial response (PR) but subsequently relapsed at month 6 after zamto-cel treatment. Thereafter, the patient was treated with Polatuzumab, Bendamustin and Rituximab and showed a CR for 3 months after succumbing to the cardiac failure.

sec.title: Cytokine analysis
sec.p: Given the high frequency of CRS, serum cytokine levels of interferon gamma, IL-6, IL-10, MCP-1, IL-2, and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) were assessed at baseline, day 0, days 1 through 6, day 9, day 14, and week 3. In patients with CRS, levels of IL-2 (tmax = time to peak concentration; tmax = day 1), IL-6 (tmax = day 9), and TNF-α (tmax = day 2) were elevated compared with patients without CRS (tmax not detectable). The other cytokines revealed inconsistent levels over time. Although IL-2 and TNF-α levels returned to baseline by day 14, IL-6 levels were still elevated in patients with CRS when compared with patients without CRS at week 3 (Figure 1B).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: The efficacy analysis included all 12 patients who received IMP infusion. At DL1, the best overall response (BOR) was 50%, with 3 patients achieving a CR. The remaining 3 patients at DL1 had stable disease as the best response and progressed subsequently. Among 6 patients at DL2, the BOR was 100%, including 2 patients with CR and 4 patients with PR. BOR for the entire study cohort was 75% (5 CR, 4 PR). The median time to first objective response was 42 days (range, 36-97), whereas the median time to CR was 105 days (range, 97-188). Based on the extended investigator assessment definition, the median progression-free survival (PFS) time was not evaluable at DL1 and 6.3 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.2 to not evaluable) at DL2. The PFS rate at month 36 was 66.7% (95% CI, 19.5-90.4) at DL1 and 33.3% (95% CI, 4.6-67.6) at DL2 (Figure 2A, PFS shown for the overall population). With a median follow-up time of 24.6 months, the OS rate at month 60 was 75.0% (95% CI, 12.8-96.1) at DL1 and 66.7% (95% CI, 5.4-94.5) at DL2 (Figure 2A, OS shown for the overall population). Among patients with CR as best response per investigator assessment, 4 of 5 patients had positron emission tomography–negative CR at month 3, whereas 1 patient converted from PR to CR at month 6 (Figure 2B). Of 5 patients in CR, all completed a 2-year follow-up visit without clinical evidence of relapse. During the follow-up period until year 5, 3 patients were lost to follow-up, and 2 patients completed the 5-year follow-up visit without any clinical evidence of relapse. All patients with PR or stable disease as the best response (n = 7) progressed within the first 180 days after infusion (Figure 2C). Of 7 patients with documented progression, 4 received a biopsy as part of the clinical routine. These available biopsies showed persistent expression of both CD19 and CD20. The median duration of response at DL2 was 4.8 months and was not reached at DL1 (Figure 2D shows DOR for the overall population).

sec.title: In vivo expansion of zamto-cel
sec.p: Because clinical response after zamto-cel was not associated with the total number of CAR+ T cells being infused, we hypothesized that in vivo expansion of zamto-cel would show better correlation with clinical response.3 To this end, we analyzed zamto-cel expansion in the peripheral blood from all 12 patients (supplemental Figure 5A). All patients with CR had a maximum observed concentration of zamto-cel (Cmax) of ≥450 cells per μL with a mean Cmax of 1092.5 cells per μL (460.1-3147.0), whereas patients without CR had significantly lower values, with a mean Cmax of 111.3 cells/μL (3.9-458.8; Figure 2E-F). The robust segregation of response by Cmax was consistent across CD4+ and CD8+ zamto-cel populations (supplemental Figure 5B). Patients without CR had a mean area under the curve from day 0 to day 28 of 944.1 days × cells per μL (28.0-3504.7), whereas the mean area under the curve from day 0 to day 28 in CR was 8245.5 days × cells per μL (95% CI, 2396.0-21 295.6; supplemental Figure 5C). Of 5 patients with CR, 2 patients still showed measurable zamto-cel concentrations above the detection limit in the peripheral blood 2 years after administration of zamto-cel. In patients without CR, no CAR T-cell concentrations above the detection limit could be determined on average after 25.4 days (95% CI, 13.0-30.0).

sec.title: Immunophenotypic analysis of exhaustion, activation, and proliferation
sec.p: Enhanced persistence of zamto-cel in some patients with CR encouraged us to next characterize DP features of zamto-cel in patients with CR vs those without CR. Thus, we profiled LP starting material and final zamto-cel DPs from patients with CR vs those without CR via flow cytometry. Immunophenotype of the DP in comparison with LP showed low expression of exhaustion markers lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3) and programmed cell death protein 1 in CD4+ and CD8+ CAR+ T cells. We observed increased CD25 expression in DPs vs LP; however, without differences between patients with and without CR. In contrast, the inducible activation marker 4-1BB was not increased on CD4+ or CD8+CAR+ cells in the DP (supplemental Figure 6A-B). Interestingly, the proliferative ability of zamto-cel as assessed by CD27 and CD127/IL-7R expression showed a trend for increased expression in patients with CR (CAR+CD4+CD27+ in CR [mean, 86.2; 95% CI, 73.57-91.59] vs non-CR [mean, 60.98; 95% CI, 8.93-92.14; P = .14], CAR+CD4+CD127/IL-7R+ in CR [mean, 82.09; 95% CI, 76.97-88.93] vs non-CR [mean, 59.34; 95% CI, 29.87-82.48; P = .035], CAR+CD8+CD27+ in CR [mean, 88.85; 95% CI, 82.09-94.46] vs non-CR [mean, 66.33; 95% CI, 16.55-94.01; P = .05] and CAR+CD8+CD127/IL-7R+ in CR [mean, 26.72; 95% CI, 15.52-43.95] vs non-CR [mean, 12.36; 95% CI, 1.93-49.96; P = .1]; Figure 3A-B; supplemental Figure 6C).

sec.title: High-dimensional profiling via single-cell RNA sequencing in zamto-cel products
sec.p: Given the higher levels of both CD27 and CD127 in zamto-cel DP from patients with CR, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of zamto-cel DP to obtain a fine-grained profile of CD27+ and CD127+ CAR+ cells. First, we validated our in silico approach to call CAR+ cells by correlating their fraction with CAR+ cells identified via flow cytometry. We found a strong correlation between in silico– and in vitro–identified CAR+ cells in zamto-cel DP (r = 1; P = .00021; supplemental Figure 7A). Next, we identified CAR+CD27+CD127+ cells in zamto-cel products (supplemental Figure 7B), which we further investigated via differential gene expression analysis. We observed genes related to protein biosynthesis (RPS28, RPS27, RPS24, EEF2, EEF1A1, RPL19, RPL30, RPS27A, RPS14, RPL10, and RPL18) and regulation of migration in naïve T cells (KLF2)33 to be highly expressed. In contrast, genes associated with cell division (KIFC1, PCLAF, TYMS, CDK1, TOP2A, CENPF, MKI67, and others) showed low expression in CAR+CD27+CD127+ cells from zamto-cel DP (Figure 3C).

sec.title: Memory subsets in DPs and during the expansion phase
sec.p: We hypothesized that the elevated expression of CD27 and CD127 yields higher levels of central memory T cells (Tcm).22,23 Therefore, we analyzed memory subsets in DPs from patients with CR and those without CR. In patients with CR, we observed higher levels of CAR+CD8+ Tcm (91.3% ± 4.7% in patients with CR vs 79.8% ± 16.3% in those without CR; Figure 3D) and CAR+CD4+ Tcm (89.8% ± 7.8% in patients with CR vs 75.2% ± 25.3% in those without CR) in DPs, whereas the cellular composition for other memory subsets was comparable in patients with CR vs those without CR (supplemental Figure 8A-B). To understand whether the higher number of Tcm cells translates into enhanced persistence, we profiled memory subsets from patients with CR vs without CR in vivo over time. Although persistence of all memory subsets in both CD4+ and CD8+ CAR T cells was improved in patients with CR (supplemental Figure 8C-D), Tcm cells showed remarkably high levels after treatment (CR, 502.7 cells per μL vs non-CR, 27 cells per μL average Cmax; Figure 3E).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The development of zamto-cel was driven by the attempt to reduce relapse in B-NHL through dual targeting of CD20 and CD19.16 Preclinical data suggest that CD19 is heterogeneously expressed in CAR T-cell–naïve B-NHL when compared with healthy B cells and thereby determines CAR activity.11 In turn, loss of the CD19 antigen after axicabtagene ciloleucel has been observed in 60% of patients with R/R B-NHL.14Genomic alterations (deletion, frameshift, and missense mutations) as well as alternative splicing of CD19 have been described in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia after treatment with CD19-directed CAR T cells.10 In contrast, in R/R DLBCL after treatment with rituximab-based chemoimmunotherapy, only 7% of cases show mutations in MS4A1 (CD20).34 Thus, the development of tandem CARs against CD19 and CD20, which signal in an “OR” gated manner resulting in sufficient CAR activation by only 1 antigen,35 provides an exciting avenue for the treatment of R/R B-NHL.

Zamto-cel was manufactured in a fully automated manner on the Miltenyi CliniMACS Prodigy closed-production system to transduce activated T cells with pLTG1497. Final products were collected after a 12-day process. Importantly, all 12 patients who underwent leukapheresis received infusion without cryopreservation. In contrast, previously tested tandem CAR T-cell products targeting CD20 and CD19 in R/R B-NHL had been manufactured either within an open process or required prolonged culture and/or cryopreservation before infusion.15,17,18 A shortened ex vivo culture has been proven to result in more naïve and memory-enriched T-cell phenotypes,36 which positively affect tumor cell killing.24 Cryopreservation results in impaired quality of final products, which negatively affects outcome.15 A prolonged ex vivo expansion as well as cryopreservation can be avoided by local manufacturing. In an academic context, on-site manufacturing is facilitated by a closed-system platform to generate good manufacturing practice–grade cell therapeutic products.37

The major AEs of CAR T-cell treatment comprise acute toxicities such as CRS and ICANS,38 but also nonimmediate hematological impairments, for example prolonged neutropenia and B-cell aplasia leading to increased rates of infection and nonrelapse mortality.39,40 Treatment with zamto-cel resulted in no DLTs, thus defining 2.5 × 106 CAR+ T cells per kg bodyweight as recommended dose for further clinical evaluation. No incidences of CRS and ICANS of grade ≥3 occurred. A comparably low rate of relevant CRS and ICANS has only been reported for 1 other tandem CAR product targeting CD20 and CD19 in R/R B-NHL.18 Only 2 patients (16.7%) showed an ongoing neutropenia of grade ≥3, which was persistent beyond day 28 (both considered not related to zamto-cel per investigator assessment), whereas thrombocytopenia, or anemia was not reported beyond day 28. Although definitions of prolonged cytopenia are not uniform across studies, one-third (30%-38%) of patients with R/R B-NHL treated with commercial anti-CD19 CAR T cells present with persistent grade ≥3 neutropenia and 21% to 29% with thrombocytopenia after day 21,39,41 resulting in significant morbidity and use of health care resources.

We observed responses in 9 patients, of whom 5 (42%) achieved a CR. None of the patients with CR progressed over the follow-up period. Although other CAR products targeting CD20 and CD19 in R/R B-NHL with comparable long-term follow-up data have achieved slightly higher overall response rates of ∼80%,15,17 durable CR was only reported in 58%42 and 70%,43 respectively. Interestingly, relapse biopsies after CD20/CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy indicated no loss of CD20 and CD19 antigens.15 CR with zamto-cel did not associate with DL but with in vivo expansion, which is in line with previous findings for axicabtagene ciloleucel in R/R B-NHL.3 These 2 findings emphasize the importance of identifying product metrics to predict successful engraftment, expansion, and persistence of tandem CD20- and CD19-directed CAR T cells in B-NHL.

Profiling final products from patients who received treatment, we identified CD27 and CD127/IL-7R overexpression in zamto-cel to be associated with CR. CD27 overexpression in CD8+ anti-CD19 CAR T-cell products has been highlighted as prognostically relevant in R/R B-NHL.22,23 When incorporated into second-generation CARs as a costimulatory domain, CD27 enhances persistence, and improves resistance against apoptosis via Bcl-XL expression.44 Naïve and Tcm express CD127/IL-7R, and stromal cells provide IL-7 to both populations for homeostatic proliferation, thereby enabling T-cell maintenance and growth despite lack of antigen- and CD28-mediated (co)stimulation.45 Hence, overexpression of CD127/IL-7R in CAR T-cell products has been hypothesized to be advantageous and to boost engraftment and expansion after lymphodepletion.46 Our high-dimensional profiling indicates that the combined expression of CD27 and CD127/IL-7R in zamto-cel is linked to a naïve state with maintained expression of ribosomes, which can immediately be engaged to facilitate the T-cell activation program.47 In patients with CR, our longitudinal analysis indicated not only enhanced expansion but also persistence, especially of central memory CAR+ T cells, and thus provides orthogonal evidence that high levels of endogenous CD127/IL-7R result in superior clinical activity of CAR T cells. Our work expands the significance of sustained memory and persistence via CD27 and CD127/IL-7R to a tandem CAR targeting R/R B-NHL and provides a direction for future development of CAR T-cell products with improved persistence in R/R B-NHL.

Our work provides evidence that zamto-cel is safe, with early signs of long-term efficacy. Given the broader activity of zamto-cel at DL2 as compared with DL1 (overall response rate of 100% vs 50%) and no additional toxicity at the higher dose, 2 pivotal phase 2 trials exploring zamto-cel efficacy at DL2 are currently being conducted: DALY 2-US studies zamto-cel as third-line therapy in R/R DLBCL, and DALY 2-EU investigates zamto-cel as second-line therapy in adult and older patients with R/R DLBCL ineligible for high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation.
